clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant axonal (type 2) sensorimotor neuropathy caused by gain-of-function variants in TRPV4, distinguished from other CMT2 subtypes by prominent respiratory and laryngeal involvement.
Vocal cord paresis with hoarseness, stridor or a weak cry, and diaphragmatic weakness are hallmark features that may dominate the presentation and can precede limb signs.
Sensorineural hearing loss occurs in a proportion of patients and, together with vocal cord and phrenic nerve involvement, points strongly to TRPV4 rather than a generic CMT2.
Nerve conduction studies show an axonal pattern with reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes and relatively preserved conduction velocities, unlike the demyelinating slowing of CMT1.

Phenotype overlaps a spectrum of allelic TRPV4 disorders, including scapuloperoneal spinal muscular atrophy and congenital distal spinal muscular atrophy, so the same gene can give motor-predominant pictures.
TRPV4 is also associated with skeletal dysplasias, and some patients or relatives show short stature or bony abnormalities, an unexpected clue in a neuropathy clinic.
Respiratory monitoring is central to management because diaphragmatic and bulbar weakness, rather than limb disability, is the principal threat to life.
Confirmation is by identifying a pathogenic TRPV4 variant; the channel is a calcium-permeable cation channel and disease alleles typically increase channel activity.
reference.pathophysiology: CMT2C is an autosomal dominant axonal neuropathy caused by heterozygous, usually gain-of-function, missense variants in TRPV4, which encodes transient receptor potential vanilloid 4, a widely expressed calcium-permeable non-selective cation channel involved in mechanosensation and osmotic and thermal sensing. Disease-associated variants, frequently clustered in the cytoplasmic ankyrin-repeat and adjacent regulatory domains, increase basal and stimulated channel activity, leading to excessive intracellular calcium entry that is thought to be toxic to motor and sensory neurons and to lower motor neuron cell bodies. This channel dysfunction produces a length-dependent axonal degeneration but also, distinctively, affects the phrenic nerve, laryngeal innervation and cochlear function, explaining the diaphragmatic weakness, vocal cord paresis and sensorineural hearing loss that characterise the subtype. The very same gene, and sometimes the very same variant, can produce allelic phenotypes ranging from scapuloperoneal spinal muscular atrophy and congenital distal spinal muscular atrophy to autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasias, illustrating pleiotropy determined by which variant and modifying factors are present.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D (GARS1) with upper-limb predominant wasting
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2E (NEFL) with axonal or intermediate features
Scapuloperoneal spinal muscular atrophy and congenital distal spinal muscular atrophy (allelic TRPV4 disorders)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or other motor neuron disease when vocal cord and respiratory weakness dominate
Distal hereditary motor neuropathies from other genes
Acquired axonal neuropathy with laryngeal involvement, including vasculitic or paraneoplastic causes
Facioscapulohumeral or other myopathies presenting with scapuloperoneal weakness
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm an axonal, length-dependent sensorimotor process with neurogenic changes
Targeted TRPV4 sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel including axonal CMT genes
Laryngoscopy to assess vocal cord movement and document paresis
Pulmonary function testing including measures sensitive to diaphragmatic weakness, and overnight oximetry or sleep study where indicated
Audiometry to detect sensorineural hearing loss
Skeletal survey or targeted imaging if features suggest an allelic bone dysplasia
Family assessment and segregation analysis given autosomal dominant inheritance and marked variability
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness, orthopnoea or nocturnal hypoventilation suggesting diaphragmatic failure
Stridor, worsening hoarseness or aspiration indicating vocal cord and bulbar compromise
Rapid deterioration in limb power or new bulbar symptoms prompting reassessment for an alternative diagnosis
Recurrent chest infections signalling inadequate airway clearance
New skeletal deformity or pain raising the possibility of an allelic bone phenotype
reference.prognosis: Disability is highly variable, ranging from mild distal weakness to severe early respiratory and bulbar compromise; life expectancy is chiefly determined by the degree of diaphragmatic and laryngeal involvement. Many patients remain ambulant, but those with significant respiratory failure require close pulmonary and airway support.
pitfalls: Attributing vocal cord paresis or hoarseness to a local ENT problem and missing the underlying hereditary neuropathy
Overlooking respiratory muscle weakness because limb strength appears relatively preserved
Labelling the picture as motor neuron disease when a treatable-monitorable inherited channelopathy is responsible
Assuming absence of family history excludes the diagnosis, as de novo variants and variable expressivity occur
Not recognising the wider TRPV4 spectrum, including skeletal dysplasia, in the patient or relatives
references: Clinical review of TRPV4-related neuromuscular disorders
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care coordinated by a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Respiratory surveillance with pulmonary function testing and overnight oximetry, with non-invasive ventilation for diaphragmatic weakness and nocturnal hypoventilation
Laryngological assessment of vocal cord paresis with airway protection, and tracheostomy where there is severe stridor or airway compromise
Audiology review and hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss
Physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for distal weakness and foot deformity
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal dominant genetic counselling and family screening, with skeletal assessment where an allelic bone dysplasia is suspected
